can we start all of the plans as planned so we don't forget them and have a way to track them with their own sessions

Brief: Plan 3 in docs/planning-handoff.md. Starter prompt from the handoff:

> Read `docs/planning-handoff.md`. Plan the quality rules engine and the local tool (Plan 3), generic first. Design the rules from what makes any dataset hard to use, then check them against the sample package from Plan 2 and the hand-made Ozone findings in `practice-data/packages/ozone-bioindicators/datapackage.json` under `archive:quality`. Then plan the commands. Take the open questions with me one at a time.

findings.text: cruise is an empty shell: argparse with --version only. Every command is still to build.

Finding has ruleId, severity (error, warning, note), message, target (resource, field, path), evidence (rows, values) and suggestedFix. Change has id, when, madeBy, acceptedBy, kind, target, before, after, reason, evidence.

Structure checks already exist and report error findings with ids under structure.*: manifest, files, sizes, hashes, checksums, foreign keys, shapefile attributes, symlinks. Plan 3's rules are about quality only.

A profile is a YAML file listing required fields and rule ids. Core lists no rules. Ecology names three placeholder rule ids: ecology.units-on-measurements, ecology.coordinates-in-range, ecology.dates-within-coverage.

The sample package has 4 planted gaps, all about column metadata or a constant column: battery_v has no description, depth_cm's description repeats its name, qc_flag codes are undocumented, logger_model is constant. None of the value problems the handoff lists (placeholders like -999, mixed date formats, swapped coordinates, merged headers, unit mix-ups) is planted.

The hand-made Ozone audit has 36 findings: 11 unit missing, 4 description missing, 3 description repeats the name, 4 type not declared, 2 type narrower than declared, 3 constant columns, 1 undocumented codes, 1 location identifier with no grid, 1 temporal gap (no 1998 rows), license, methods and spatial coverage missing, taxonomic coverage missing, plus 2 about the source EML (the distibution tag, a trailing space in the title).
The Ozone findings used dotted codes such as column.description.missing and evidence shapes the contract's Evidence can't hold (distinctCount, inferredType, yearsPresent, value with a row count).
The contract has no taxonomic coverage field, so Ozone's 'taxonomic coverage missing' finding has nothing to check yet.
Every species column in the practice data holds numeric codes, not names: Ozone SPECIES (6 codes), FIA SPCD (76 codes), aerial survey HOST1 (536 values).

rounds.take:
**Where Plan 3 starts.** Plan 2 left a contract with Finding and Change models, structure checks under `structure.*`, profiles that switch rules on by id, and a sample package with four planted gaps. `cruise` itself is empty. So Plan 3 builds the quality rules, then the commands on top of them.

**My take on the rules: organise them by the question a reader can't answer.** A dataset is hard to use when you can't tell what it is, can't tell what a column means, or can't trust the values. That gives three groups, each a set of small deterministic checks:

1. **Can I find, cite and reuse it?** (the package): core fields missing (already `missing_core_fields`), fields a profile requires missing (methods, coverage), rights.
2. **Can I understand each column?** (the schema): no description, a description that only repeats the name, a measurement with no unit, codes with no code list, a type guessed rather than declared.
3. **Can I trust the values?** (the data, read with DuckDB): constant columns, placeholder values such as -999 that aren't declared missing, mixed date formats, dates outside the stated coverage or gaps in it, coordinates out of range or swapped, duplicate keys.

Each rule is a Python function in `cruise` with a stable dotted id (`field.description-missing`, `values.placeholder`), a default severity, and what it looks at (package, column, or table rows). A profile switches rules on by id, as the ecology profile already does; I'd rename its three placeholders into this scheme. Structure stays in the contract as Plan 2 built it.

**Checked against the two tests** (table below): the first two groups and the constant-column rule catch all 4 planted gaps in the sample and 26 of Ozone's 36. Of the other 10, 6 are about types guessed at import and 2 about FEMC's EML (both belong to import, Plan 5), 1 needs a taxonomic coverage field the contract lacks, and 1 is a judgement call (a column that looks like a grid id). **The gap:** neither test holds a single value problem, so the third group, the one the handoff's rule list is mostly about, would have nothing to prove itself on. I'd add a small messy fixture with planted value problems.

**Build order.** The commands split cleanly into three plans, each usable on its own:

1. Rules engine, the first rule set, and `cruise diagnose` (one package) and `cruise audit` (many, ranked), proven on the sample, the messy fixture and Ozone.
2. `cruise tidy` (proposals written to `changes.jsonl`, originals untouched) and `cruise package` (build the folder, checksums, README).
3. `cruise inventory` and `cruise profile` for a messy folder before it is a package.

Open questions for later, one at a time: what blocks versus warns, how the completeness score works, offline species lookups, and how far inventory goes without an agent.

rounds.recommendation: Rules grouped by the three reader questions (find and cite, understand each column, trust the values), each a Python function in cruise with a dotted id, default severity and scope, value checks in DuckDB, profiles switching them on by id; a small messy fixture added so the value rules have cases; built as three plans: rules plus diagnose and audit first, then tidy and package, then inventory and profile.

points.text: A local-first command line tool, cruise, that cleans, organizes and packages data, built on a rules engine that produces graded findings with evidence.

Rules designed generically from what makes any dataset hard to use: can I find and cite it, can I understand each column, can I trust the values. Nothing in the core is specific to FEMC or ecology; ecology adds rules through its profile.
The commands: inventory, profile, diagnose, tidy, package and audit. Audit runs over many packages and ranks them by what needs fixing.
Built as three plans, each usable on its own: rules plus diagnose and audit; then tidy and package; then inventory and profile.
Local-first, state on disk, no network needed, no phoning home. Checks are deterministic code; an agent is optional and handles judgement calls only.
Tidy is a proposal with a reviewable change log in changes.jsonl. Originals are never modified.
DuckDB reads tables, CSV now and Parquet later, through one interface.
Plan 2's Finding and Change models are confirmed or changed here, as an edit to the contract. Structure checks stay in the contract as Plan 2 built them.
The rules produce the sample package's 4 planted findings, and Ozone's hand-made findings are a second test.
A small messy fixture with planted value problems (placeholders, mixed dates, bad coordinates, duplicate keys) gives each value rule a case it must catch.
Every check runs with the network off.

decisions.name: What blocks publishing
decisions.question: Which findings stop a package from being published, and which only warn?
decisions.example: Ozone Bioindicators (one of the FEMC practice datasets, converted by hand) has 4 columns with no description. If a missing description blocks, Ozone can't be published until someone writes 4 definitions FEMC never recorded; if it only warns, Ozone publishes with the warning shown on its page and in review.

options.title: Only required fields and structure block
options.includes: Severity gets a fixed meaning: error = blocks publishing (structure errors, core fields missing, a field the deployment's profiles require missing, rights undetermined); warning = makes the data hard to use (column and value rules); note = worth knowing. No column or value rule is ever an error.
options.pulls_in: Nothing new: the blockers are exactly what the contract and profiles already call required.

options.title: Every error-severity finding blocks
options.includes: Rules carry their own severity, as in the Ozone draft, and some column rules (description missing, undocumented codes) are errors that block.
options.pulls_in: Most legacy data can't publish until its gaps are filled; Plan 5's migration would stall on gaps the source never recorded.

options.title: Nothing blocks automatically
options.includes: Findings are advice only; the curator in review (Plan 7) decides every package.
options.pulls_in: A package with no license or no title could reach review and be approved by mistake, against Plan 2's rights decision.

options.title: A, plus one list of blocking rules per archive
options.includes: A as the default, and the archive config can name rule ids that block everything that archive receives (for example field.description-missing). Old and new packages in the same archive get the same list.
options.pulls_in: A blocking-rules list in the archive config model (a contract edit) and in Plan 7's ingest. FEMC's migrated records would be blocked by the same list as new submissions.

options.title: A, plus rules that block new submissions only
options.includes: A as the default, and the archive config can name rule ids that block new submissions. A package migrated from an earlier system, which carries archive:legacyIdentifiers, gets those rules as warnings. Review shows the curator which treatment a package got.
options.pulls_in: The same config list and ingest check as D, plus the legacy test. Anyone could add a legacy identifier to dodge the stricter rules, so the curator checks it in review.

recommendation.why: It gives severity one meaning everyone can predict, keeps Plan 2's rule that undetermined rights can't publish, and lets real legacy data in with its gaps visible rather than stuck: blocking can't recover a definition nobody recorded. No archive has asked for a stricter list yet; if FEMC wants new submissions held to more, E is the one that fits an archive holding both old and new data, and it can be added later on top of A.

approved.body:
# Quality rules, cruise diagnose and cruise audit

## Goal

A researcher or curator runs `cruise diagnose` on a package folder and gets a clear list of what makes the data hard to use, each problem backed by evidence (which column, which rows, which values), plus a completeness score and whether anything blocks publishing. `cruise audit` runs the same checks over many packages and ranks them by what needs fixing. Everything runs on the user's own machine with no network.

This is the first useful piece of the local tool. Fixing problems (`tidy`), building packages (`package`) and sorting a messy folder (`inventory`, `profile`) are planned later in this folder, once diagnose has been used on real data.

**Risk.** Low. diagnose and audit only read: they never change a package, so a wrong rule produces a wrong finding, never lost data. A mistake is undone by fixing the rule. The two contract edits add optional fields, so existing packages still parse.

**Cost.** No new programs for the user and no steps they must do. One new Python dependency, DuckDB, in cruise.

## What diagnose and audit do

`cruise diagnose <package-folder>`:

1. Runs Plan 2's structure check (`validate_package`). If the manifest can't be read, it stops there and reports why.
2. Runs every quality rule that applies, skipping the data rules on any resource whose files failed the structure check.
3. Prints the findings grouped by the three questions below, each with its evidence and, where there is one, a suggested fix; then the score with its three parts; then a one-line verdict: "blocks publishing (3)" or "publishable, with 12 warnings".
4. With `--json`, prints the same as one JSON object: the structure verdict, the quality verdict with the score, and every finding in the contract's `Finding` shape.
5. Exits 1 when any finding blocks publishing, else 0, so scripts and CI can use it.

Which profiles apply comes from `--config <archive.yaml>` (the archive config, which names profiles and extra required fields) or from `--profile <name>`, repeatable. With neither, only core applies.

`cruise audit <folder>`:

1. Finds every `datapackage.json` under the folder and runs diagnose on each.
2. Prints one row per package, ranked by blockers (most first), then by score (lowest first): package, blockers, warnings, notes, score and its three parts, and the rule that fired most.
3. With `--json`, prints the rows plus every package's findings.

Neither command writes anything. Recording the verdict in a package's manifest belongs to `cruise package`, later.

Rests on: AGNT7, DCSN1, DCSN2

## The rules

The rules are grouped by the question a reader can't answer. Each is small, deterministic code with a stable id.

**Can I find, cite and reuse it?** (the package)

| Rule | Catches | Severity |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `package.core-missing` | A core field missing: title, a description of at least 50 characters, a creator, rights (a license or a stated rights status other than undetermined), a described resource. One finding per field, from Plan 2's `missing_core_fields`. | error |
| `package.profile-field-missing` | A field the selected profiles or the archive config require, such as methods or coverage under ecology. One finding per field. | error |

**Can I understand each column?** (every column of a table, and every attribute of a vector resource)

| Rule | Catches | Severity |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `field.description-missing` | No description. | warning |
| `field.description-repeats-name` | A description that only repeats the column's name or source name, ignoring case, spaces and punctuation. | warning |
| `field.unit-missing` | A number or integer column on an interval or ratio scale, or with no scale stated, that has no `archive:unit`. | warning |
| `field.codes-undocumented` | A column marked `archive:codeList: "undocumented"`. The evidence lists its distinct values, up to 20. | warning |

**Can I trust the values?** (table resources, read with DuckDB)

| Rule | Catches | Severity |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `values.not-declared-type` | Values that don't read as the column's declared type and aren't declared missing, such as `n/a` in an integer column. | warning |
| `values.placeholder` | A number column holding a placeholder that isn't declared missing: one of -9999, -999, -99, 9999, 99999, or a negative value that repeats in a column whose other values are all zero or more (the aerial survey's `-1` in HOST1). | warning |
| `values.constant` | A column with one value in every row (more than one row). | warning |
| `values.mixed-date-formats` | A string column whose values parse as dates in more than one pattern, such as `2024-06-01` and `06/01/2024`. | warning |
| `values.dates-outside-coverage` | Values in a date, datetime or year column outside the package's temporal coverage. | warning |
| `values.coverage-gap` | A whole year inside the temporal coverage with no rows (Ozone's 1998). | note |
| `values.coordinates-out-of-range` | Latitudes beyond ±90 or longitudes beyond ±180, in a geopoint column or in columns named for latitude and longitude; when the values fit the other axis's range, the finding says they look swapped. Also values outside the package's spatial coverage box. | warning |
| `values.duplicate-key` | Rows that repeat the table's primary key. | warning |

Every finding names its target (resource and column) and carries evidence: row numbers (up to 20), the values, and how many rows show it.

Species-name matching against ITIS is not in this set: every species column in the practice data holds numeric codes, which the code-list rule covers.

Rests on: AGNT2, DCSN1, DCSN3

## What blocks publishing

Severity has one meaning everywhere:

- **error** blocks publishing: Plan 2's structure errors, `package.core-missing` and `package.profile-field-missing`.
- **warning** makes the data hard to use: every column and value rule.
- **note** is worth knowing: `values.coverage-gap`.

No column or value rule is ever an error, so legacy data with gaps it can't fill can still be published, with the gaps shown. diagnose's verdict and exit code follow from this; Plan 7's ingest uses the same rule.

Rests on: DCSN1

## The completeness score

A check is one rule applied to one target: `field.description-missing` on a 17-column table is 17 checks; `package.core-missing` is 5 checks, one per core field. A check passes when the rule finds nothing on that target. Value rules count one check per column they look at.

The score is the share of checks passed, as a whole percent rounded down, with no weights, overall and for each of the three questions. diagnose shows it as `61% (find 4 of 7, understand 21 of 51, trust 30 of 34)`, so anyone can recount it. Structure errors are not in the score: they block, and are shown on their own.

audit ranks by blockers first, then by lowest score, so packages of different sizes compare fairly: a 207-column table isn't ranked worse just for having more columns.

Rests on: DCSN2

## How the rules are built

- The rules live in a `cruise.rules` module that imports without the command line, so the archive's ingest (Plan 7) and the MCP server (Plan 9) can run the same rules by depending on cruise as a library.
- A rule is a Python function registered with its id, its question (find, understand or trust), what it looks at (the package, each column, or each table's rows) and its severity. It returns findings.
- Core rules always run. A profile can switch on extra rules by id through its `rules` list; no profile has any yet.
- Tables are read through one function backed by DuckDB, given a resource. It is the only place a file format appears, so Parquet later is one more branch there. CSV files are read as text and each value rule tests casts in SQL, so a bad value becomes a finding rather than a failed read.
- No rule touches the network. A test runs diagnose with network access disabled.

Rests on: AGNT1, AGNT2

## Changes to the contract

- `Evidence` gains `count`: how many rows show the problem, since a finding like "18,104 rows hold -1" can't list them all. `Finding` and `Change` are otherwise confirmed as Plan 2 drafted them.
- `QualityVerdict` gains the score: `score` (0 to 100) and, for each of find, understand and trust, the checks passed and applicable. All optional, so manifests without them still parse.
- `ecology.yaml`'s three placeholder rules become core rules (`field.unit-missing`, `values.dates-outside-coverage`, `values.coordinates-out-of-range`), since none is specific to ecology, and its `rules` list is emptied.
- The web app's JSON Schema is regenerated from the changed models, as Plan 2's check requires.

Rests on: AGNT2, AGNT3, DCSN2

## Test data

- **The sample package** (Plan 2) must give exactly its 4 planted findings and no others: `field.description-missing` on battery_v, `field.description-repeats-name` on depth_cm, `field.codes-undocumented` on qc_flag, `values.constant` on logger_model.
- **A messy test package**, new, beside cruise's tests: small, invented, structurally valid, with each value problem planted once and listed in its GAPS.md (a placeholder, a value of the wrong type, two date formats, a date outside coverage, a missing year, swapped and out-of-range coordinates, a duplicate key, a measurement with no unit), plus a missing license and missing methods under ecology so the blockers show.
- **Ozone** is checked on paper: the rule list catches 26 of its 36 hand-made findings; the other 10 are about building the package or FEMC's EML (8), a field the contract lacks (1) and a judgement call (1). A real diagnose run on Ozone waits on Plan 5 converting it, since the hand-made package uses an early draft of the format.

Rests on: AGNT4, AGNT8

## Left out

- `cruise tidy` and `cruise package`: the next plan in this folder, planned after diagnose has been used (follow-up PARK3). Calls AGNT5 (types inferred when packaging) and AGNT6 (tidy proposals wait in `_build/`) are its starting point.
- `cruise inventory` and `cruise profile`, and how far inventory groups files without an agent: after that (PARK4).
- Species-name matching against ITIS (PARK5).
- A taxonomic coverage field in the contract (PARK1), and spotting a grid id with no grid described, which is a judgement call for the agent layer (PARK2).
- Writing the verdict into a package's manifest: `cruise package` does it later.
- A per-archive or new-submissions-only list of extra blocking rules (options D and E of DCSN1): addable later on top of this.
- Running on Ozone and the other FEMC data: Plan 5.

Rests on: AGNT5, AGNT6, AGNT7, DCSN1, DCSN3

## How we'll know it works

1. `cruise diagnose examples/sample-package` prints exactly the 4 planted findings, no blockers, a score, and exits 0.
2. `cruise diagnose` on the messy test package prints one finding for each planted problem in its GAPS.md and no others, reports 2 blockers, and exits 1.
3. `cruise audit` over a folder holding both packages ranks the messy package first.
4. `--json` output from both commands validates against the contract's `Finding` model.
5. The diagnose tests pass with network access disabled.
6. The repo's existing checks (`just check`, as CI runs it) pass, including the regenerated JSON Schema.

Rests on: AGNT4, AGNT8

approved.body:
# PLAN1: The rules, cruise diagnose and cruise audit

## Spec

`docs/specs/2026-11-13-quality-rules-and-local-tool/spec.md`, all of it: this plan builds everything the spec covers.

## The change

- Two small contract edits: `Evidence.count`, and the score on `QualityVerdict`. The ecology profile's three placeholder rules move into core.
- In cruise: a rules module with the 14 rules, one DuckDB-backed table reader, the score, `cruise diagnose` and `cruise audit`.
- A small messy test package that plants each value problem once.

**Risk.** Low. Both commands only read, and the contract edits add optional fields. A wrong rule gives a wrong finding and is undone by fixing the rule.

**Cost.** No steps for the user. One new dependency, `duckdb`, in cruise.

**Gates, sized to that risk.** CI's own commands (`just check-python` and `just check-schema`) and the tests each task names. One review at the end by a reviewer from the other provider family. No stress or fuzz runs.

## Left out

- `tidy`, `package`, `inventory` and `profile`: later plans in this folder (PARK3, PARK4).
- Species names against ITIS (PARK5), a taxonomic coverage field (PARK1), grid ids (PARK2).
- Writing the verdict into a manifest.
- Extra blocking rules per archive (DCSN1 options D and E).
- A run on Ozone or other FEMC data: Plan 5.

## Where

- Repo: `schuettc/research-in-a-box`, base branch `main`.
- Branch `plan3/diagnose-and-audit`, in the worktree `/Users/courtschuett/GitHub/personal/.worktrees/research-archive-in-a-box/plan3/diagnose-and-audit`. The branch already holds this planning folder's commit.
- Contract: `packages/contract/src/archive_contract/`.
- Tool: `packages/tool/src/cruise/`, tests in `packages/tool/tests/`.
- One pull request for the whole plan, with auto-merge on once CI is green.

### Task 1: Contract edits

**Does:** Adds `count` to `Evidence` and the score to `QualityVerdict`, and moves the ecology profile's placeholder rules into core. Then regenerates the web app's JSON Schema.
**Files:** `packages/contract/src/archive_contract/findings.py`, `manifest.py`, `profiles/ecology.yaml`, `packages/contract/tests/test_findings.py`, `test_manifest.py`, `test_profile.py`, `packages/web/src/schema/archive-contract.schema.json`
**Checks:** `just check-python`, `just check-schema`
**Serves:** DCSN2 (rests on calls AGNT2, AGNT3)

- `Evidence.count: NonNegativeInt | None`.
- A `CheckCount` model (`passed`, `applicable`, both non-negative ints, passed ≤ applicable).
- `QualityVerdict` gains `score: int | None` (0 to 100) and `find`, `understand` and `trust`, each a `CheckCount | None`. All optional, so existing manifests still parse. Add a test that the sample package's manifest still loads.
- `ecology.yaml`: empty its `rules` list and replace the placeholder comment with one line saying the units, coverage-date and coordinate checks are core rules.
- Regenerate the schema with `just schema`.

### Task 2: Rules engine, package and column rules, cruise diagnose

**Does:** Builds the rule registry, the table reader, the 6 package and column rules, the score and `cruise diagnose`, proven on the sample package.
**Files:** `packages/tool/pyproject.toml` (add `duckdb`), `uv.lock`, `packages/tool/src/cruise/rules/__init__.py`, `rules/registry.py`, `rules/package.py`, `rules/fields.py`, `tables.py`, `score.py`, `diagnose.py`, `cli.py`, `packages/tool/tests/test_rules_package.py`, `test_rules_fields.py`, `test_diagnose.py`, `test_cli.py`
**Checks:** `just check-python`; `uv run cruise diagnose examples/sample-package` exits 0
**Serves:** DCSN1, DCSN2 (rests on calls AGNT1, AGNT2, AGNT7)

- **Registry.** A rule is a function registered with a decorator giving its id, its question (`find`, `understand`, `trust`), what it looks at (`package`, `field` or `table`) and its severity. It receives a context (the package root, the `Manifest`, the required fields from the selected profiles and config, and the table reader) and returns `Finding`s plus the number of checks it applied, so the score can count passes.
- **Required fields** are the union of each selected profile's `required` and the archive config's `required`, minus the core fields, which `package.core-missing` covers.
- **Profiles.** Core rules always run; a profile's `rules` list switches on extra registered rules by id, and an unknown id is an error.
- **`cruise.rules` imports without the CLI** (no argparse in it), so Plan 7 and Plan 9 can import it.
- **The rules this task builds:** `package.core-missing` (one finding per id from `missing_core_fields`), `package.profile-field-missing`, `field.description-missing`, `field.description-repeats-name`, `field.unit-missing` and `field.codes-undocumented`, exactly as the spec's tables define them. Field rules run over every table column and every vector attribute.
- **`tables.py`.** One function: given the root and a table resource, return a DuckDB relation over its file read as text (`all_varchar`), with the schema's missing values known. It refuses any format but `csv` with a clear error. It is the only place a format appears.
- **`score.py`.** The share of checks passed, rounded down to a whole percent, overall and per question, as in the spec. Structure findings are excluded.
- **`diagnose.py`.**
  - Runs `validate_package` first and stops if the manifest can't be read.
  - Skips table rules on resources with structure findings.
  - Returns the findings (structure first) and a `QualityVerdict` with the score.
- **CLI.** `cruise diagnose <folder> [--json] [--profile NAME]... [--config FILE]`.
  - Text output is grouped by question, each finding with its target, evidence and suggested fix, then the score line and the verdict line.
  - `--json` prints `{"validation": ..., "quality": ..., "findings": [...]}` from the contract models.
  - Exit 1 when any finding is an error, else 0.
- **Tests.**
  - The sample package gives exactly 4 findings: battery_v, depth_cm and qc_flag here, and logger_model's `values.constant` in Task 3. Until then, assert the 3 column findings and no others from this task's rules.
  - A test runs diagnose with `socket.socket` patched to raise, and it still passes.
  - `--json` output round-trips through `Finding`.

### Task 3: The messy test package and the value rules

**Does:** Adds the messy test package and the 8 value rules. diagnose then gives exactly the planted findings on both packages.
**Files:** `packages/tool/tests/fixtures/messy-package/` (`datapackage.json`, `data/*.csv`, `checksums.sha256`, `_build/GAPS.md`, `_build/make.py`), `packages/tool/src/cruise/rules/values.py`, `packages/tool/tests/test_rules_values.py`, `test_diagnose.py`
**Checks:** `just check-python`; `uv run cruise diagnose packages/tool/tests/fixtures/messy-package --profile ecology` exits 1
**Serves:** DCSN1 (rests on calls AGNT4, AGNT2)

- **The value rules:** `values.not-declared-type`, `values.placeholder`, `values.constant`, `values.mixed-date-formats`, `values.dates-outside-coverage`, `values.coverage-gap` (note), `values.coordinates-out-of-range` and `values.duplicate-key`.
  - Each works as the spec's table says, in DuckDB SQL over the text relation from `tables.py`, testing casts with `TRY_CAST`.
  - Evidence gives up to 20 row numbers (1-based data rows), the values, and `count`.
  - Coordinates are found by a `geopoint` type or by column names (`lat`, `latitude`, `lon`, `long`, `longitude`, any case).
  - Dates are checked against `archive:temporalCoverage`; with `ongoing`, only the start bounds them.
- **The messy package:**
  - Invented and small: one table of about 40 rows, one code list. It must be structurally valid (`validate_package` returns nothing); `_build/make.py` writes the files, sizes, hashes and checksums, as the sample package's own `make.py` does.
  - Plant exactly once each: a `-999` in a number column; an `n/a` in an integer column; a string date column with two formats; a date before the coverage start; a year inside the coverage with no rows; one row with latitude and longitude swapped and one latitude of 95; a repeated primary key; a ratio column with no unit.
  - No license and no `archive:methods`, so under `--profile ecology` there are exactly 2 blockers. Every other column is described and has a unit, so nothing unplanted fires.
  - `_build/GAPS.md` lists each planted problem with the rule id it must trigger.
- **Tests.**
  - The messy package gives exactly the GAPS.md findings: rule id and target, no more and no fewer.
  - The sample package now gives exactly its 4 planted findings.
  - Each value rule has a focused unit test on a tiny in-memory table.

### Task 4: cruise audit

**Does:** Builds `cruise audit`: diagnose over every package under a folder, ranked.
**Files:** `packages/tool/src/cruise/audit.py`, `cli.py`, `packages/tool/tests/test_audit.py`
**Checks:** `just check-python`; `uv run cruise audit packages/tool/tests/fixtures examples` lists the messy package first
**Serves:** DCSN2 (rests on call AGNT7)

- Finds every `datapackage.json` under the folders given, skipping `_build/` and `node_modules/`, and runs diagnose on each, with the same `--profile` and `--config` options.
- Text output: one row per package, ranked by error count (most first), then score (lowest first), then path. Columns: path, errors, warnings, notes, score with its three parts, and the rule that fired most.
- `--json` prints the rows and each package's findings. Exit 0 unless a folder doesn't exist.
- A package whose manifest can't be read is listed first, with its structure error.
- Tests: the ranking order on the two packages plus a broken copy made in a temp folder; `--json` round-trips through `Finding`.

messages.text: From Plan 2 (package format and contract), built and merged on main in schuettc/research-in-a-box (#1, #3, #4). Two things for you. (1) The Change and Finding models are drafted in packages/contract/src/archive_contract/changes.py and findings.py (spec section "The change log and findings"); Plan 2's call AGNT10 says you confirm or change them when you start, as an edit to the contract. (2) Hooks for rules: missing_core_fields(manifest) in manifest.py; validate_package(path) returns structure.* error Findings; the ecology profile names three placeholder rule ids that are yours to define; new optional fields you may want rules for are archive:unit, archive:measurementScale, archive:codeList "undocumented", archive:ancillaryOf and archive:attributes. The sample package's seeded gaps are listed in examples/sample-package/_build/GAPS.md.

"Ozone" is short for Ozone Bioindicators, one of the six FEMC datasets downloaded into practice-data/. It's a small table: 165 rows and 17 columns of plant-injury scores from ozone exposure, 1997 to 2001. It was converted by hand into our package format before Plan 2, and that conversion came with a hand-made quality check of 36 findings (in practice-data/packages/ozone-bioindicators/datapackage.json under archive:quality). That's why I use it as the second test for the rules, after the sample package.

For this card: Ozone has 4 columns with no description at all. Under A (my recommendation), those are warnings and Ozone can still be published with them showing. Only its missing license, missing methods and missing spatial coverage would block it.
is the data useful if the columns don't have descriptions?  or are they generally optional?

Good question. In the standards, column descriptions are optional in Frictionless but required in EML: every EML attribute needs an attributeDefinition. Plan 2's EML export writes a NO_DEFINITION placeholder when one is missing, so the export stays valid but says nothing.

How much a missing description hurts depends on the column. Ozone's four undescribed columns: ID and PROJECT hold the same value in every row, so they tell you almost nothing either way. HEXAGONNUMBER is a location id that's useless until someone says which grid it belongs to. PLOTNUMBER you can mostly guess. So the data is still usable but weaker, and the knowledge to fill the gap is often gone for legacy data.

That's why I lean to warnings: blocking wouldn't produce descriptions for old data, it would only keep the data unpublished. But your question points at a real middle ground, so I've added option D: each deployment lists in its archive config which rules block. An archive taking new submissions could require every column described, while a migration of old records leaves it a warning. I still recommend A because no deployment has asked for D yet, and it can be added later without changing anything in A.
is D block for new data and warn for old data?

Not quite. D as I wrote it is per archive: one list of blocking rules for everything that archive receives. FEMC is a single archive holding both its old records and any new submissions, so under D both would get the same list: block both or warn on both.

"Block for new, warn for old" needs each package to say whether it's old. The contract already has a fair signal for that: a package migrated from an earlier system carries archive:legacyIdentifiers (its EML package id and so on), and a fresh submission doesn't. I've added that as option E: the archive config names the rules that block new submissions, and a package with legacy identifiers gets those rules as warnings only. The catch is that anyone could add a legacy identifier to dodge the rules, so the curator sees it in review.

My recommendation is still A for now, since no archive has a stricter list yet. If you expect FEMC to want "describe every column" for new submissions, E fits better than D.
what is the completelness score used for?

The handoff puts a score in scope without saying who uses it, so here are the uses I can see in the plans:

1. **Audit ranking** (this plan): `cruise audit` runs over many packages and ranks them by what needs fixing.
2. **The FEMC report** (Plan 10b): its rule is that counts come from the audit tool, so a line like "the median package is 58% complete; 3 of 6 have no license" would come from here.
3. **Progress while cleaning**: `cruise diagnose` before and after tidying shows 61% → 84%, and the same findings show on the web app's submission screen (Plan 8).

Raw counts handle most of this. The score adds one thing counts can't: a fair comparison between packages of different sizes. FIA has 207 columns and Ozone has 17, so FIA will always have more warnings even if it's better described. A share of checks passed takes size out of it. That's why I recommend B over A.

If you don't see yourself or FEMC using a single number, A (counts plus per-question checklists like "10 of 17 columns described") is the smaller option and loses only that size-fair comparison.

From the coordinating session for research-in-a-box. Court asked that every planning session know this. Muster alias: personal-personal/generic-package-format-and-contract (the name is left over from Plan 2; this session now coordinates all the plans).

1. Send cross-plan questions here first: anything that touches another plan's interface, ownership or order, or the overall direction. Ask over muster or with diazo_note to this alias. Questions only Court can answer still go on your own page as decision cards.
2. Send a one-line muster message here when your understanding is confirmed, your spec is printed, each plan is printed, and the build is done. I check each spec and plan for scope before Court approves it.
3. Record anything other plans rely on in the Decision log of docs/planning-handoff.md.
4. Keep it small. Plans 1 and 2 are built: the repo, the uv and npm workspaces, archive_contract, the exports and the sample package. Build on them and don't rebuild. Plan only what your brief needs to work end to end now, and put everything else in follow-ups. Size checks to the risk. Question every option, config field and fallback that no real case needs yet.
5. FEMC is the test afterwards, never the source of the design (Plan 2's PRIN1).
